description: The mathematics behind programming, computing, finance, business, and economics — one question at a time. Think it through, then choose A, B, or C, and move on at your own pace.

questions.learningObjective: Count committee selections that require choosing a fixed number of members from each of two separate groups.
questions.question: A team of 5 people is chosen from a pool of 6 editors and 5 illustrators, requiring exactly 2 editors and 3 illustrators. How many different teams are possible?
questions.explanation: Choose from each group independently and multiply: C(6,2) × C(5,3) = 15 × 10 = 150.

questions.learningObjective: Count the number of ways to arrange n distinct objects in a row.

questions.explanation: Arranging 6 distinct objects in a row uses all 6 positions, so the count is 6! = 720.

questions.explanation: Give each of the 5 students one item first (using up 5 items), leaving 11 items to distribute freely among 5 students: C((11)+5−1, 5−1) = C(15,4) = 1365.

questions.concept: Counting sequences with a recurrence relation
questions.learningObjective: Count binary strings avoiding a forbidden pattern by building a recurrence relation.
questions.question: How many on/off signal sequences of length 11 contain no two consecutive 1s?
questions.explanation: Let f(n) count valid strings of length n. A valid string either ends in 0 (preceded by any valid string of length n−1) or ends in 01 (preceded by any valid string of length n−2), giving f(n) = f(n−1) + f(n−2). Starting from f(1)=2 and f(2)=3 and applying this recurrence up to n = 11 gives f(11) = 233.
questions.hint: Build a recurrence: a valid string of length n either ends in 0 or ends in 01, linking it back to shorter valid strings.

questions.question: 10 sprinters compete in a race. In how many different ways can 1st and 2nd place be awarded, assuming no ties?
questions.explanation: Since the order of the 2 places matters, the count is P(10,2) = 10!/(10-2)! = 90.
questions.hint: When order matters (1st place differs from 2nd place), use the permutation formula P(n,r) = n!/(n−r)!.

questions.concept: Counting sequences with a recurrence relation
questions.learningObjective: Count binary strings avoiding a forbidden pattern by building a recurrence relation.
questions.question: How many binary strings of length 10 contain no two consecutive 1s?
questions.explanation: Let f(n) count valid strings of length n. A valid string either ends in 0 (preceded by any valid string of length n−1) or ends in 01 (preceded by any valid string of length n−2), giving f(n) = f(n−1) + f(n−2). Starting from f(1)=2 and f(2)=3 and applying this recurrence up to n = 10 gives f(10) = 144.
questions.hint: Build a recurrence: a valid string of length n either ends in 0 or ends in 01, linking it back to shorter valid strings.

questions.concept: Permutations of r objects chosen from n

questions.hint: Compute all circular arrangements, then subtract the ones where the restricted pair sits together.

questions.explanation: Since the order of the 3 places matters, the count is P(12,3) = 12!/(12-3)! = 1320.

A valid string either ends in 0 (preceded by any valid string of length n−1) or ends in 01 (preceded by any valid string of length n−2), giving f(n) = f(n−1) + f(n−2). Starting from f(1)=2 and f(2)=3 and applying this recurrence up to n = 5 gives f(5) = 13.

questions.explanation: With 6 colors, it's possible to pull 6 umbrellas and have one of each color with no match. Pulling one more (6+1 = 7) guarantees, by the pigeonhole principle, that at least two share a color.
questions.hint: Consider the worst case where you pick one of every color first, then add one more to force a repeat.

questions.learningObjective: Count distinct arrangements of a sequence with three groups of repeated symbols using the multinomial coefficient.
questions.question: A sequence of 9 symbols is formed using one symbol repeated 2 times, a second symbol repeated 3 times, and a third symbol repeated 4 times. How many distinct sequences can be formed?
questions.explanation: Using the multinomial coefficient, the number of distinct arrangements is 9!/(2!×3!×4!) = 1260.
questions.hint: Divide the factorial of the total length by the factorial of each repeated group's size (the multinomial coefficient).

questions.concept: Counting sequences with a recurrence relation
questions.learningObjective: Count binary strings avoiding a forbidden pattern by building a recurrence relation.
questions.question: How many binary strings of length 14 contain no two consecutive 1s?
questions.explanation: Let f(n) count valid strings of length n. A valid string either ends in 0 (preceded by any valid string of length n−1) or ends in 01 (preceded by any valid string of length n−2), giving f(n) = f(n−1) + f(n−2). Starting from f(1)=2 and f(2)=3 and applying this recurrence up to n = 14 gives f(14) = 987.
questions.hint: Build a recurrence: a valid string of length n either ends in 0 or ends in 01, linking it back to shorter valid strings.

questions.learningObjective: Count selections of a fixed size that must include one specific, predetermined object.
questions.question: A panel of 6 people is chosen from a squad of 9, and one specific senior member must always be included. How many different panels are possible?
questions.explanation: Since that member's spot is fixed, only 5 more people need to be chosen from the remaining 8 squad members: C(8,5) = 56.
questions.hint: Since one member is already guaranteed a spot, only choose the remaining spots from everyone else.

questions.learningObjective: Count the number of sequences where each position has the same number of independent choices and repetition is allowed.
questions.question: A voicemail passcode consists of 7 digits, each chosen from 0 through 9. Digits may repeat. How many different voicemail passcodes are possible?
questions.explanation: Each of the 7 positions can independently be any of 10 digits, so the total count is 10^7 = 10000000.
questions.hint: Since digits can repeat, multiply the number of choices for each position together: 10 raised to the number of positions.

questions.learningObjective: Use the inclusion–exclusion principle to count the union of two overlapping sets.
questions.question: In a group of 44 students, 14 students do French and 14 students do Spanish. If 6 students do both, how many students do at least one of the two activities?
questions.explanation: By inclusion–exclusion, |A∪B| = |A| + |B| − |A∩B| = 14 + 14 − 6 = 22.
questions.hint: Add the two group sizes, then subtract the overlap once so it isn't counted twice.

questions.learningObjective: Apply Pascal's identity C(n,r) = C(n−1,r−1) + C(n−1,r) to compute a binomial coefficient.
questions.question: Given that C(10,3) = 120 and C(10,4) = 210, use Pascal's identity to find C(11,4).
questions.explanation: Pascal's identity states C(n,r) = C(n−1,r−1) + C(n−1,r). Substituting the given values: C(11,4) = 120 + 210 = 330.
questions.hint: Pascal's identity says each entry equals the sum of the two entries above it: C(n,r) = C(n−1,r−1) + C(n−1,r).

questions.learningObjective: Combine circular permutation counting with complementary counting to exclude a forbidden adjacency.
questions.question: 6 delegates, including Sofia and Aiko, sit around a circular table (rotations count as the same arrangement). In how many ways can they be seated so that Sofia and Aiko do NOT sit next to each other?
questions.explanation: Total circular arrangements: (6−1)! = 120. Arrangements with Sofia and Aiko adjacent: glue them into one block, leaving 5 units around the circle in (4)! ways, times 2 for their internal order: 48. Subtracting: 120 − 48 = 72.
questions.hint: Compute all circular arrangements, then subtract the ones where the restricted pair sits together.

questions.learningObjective: Count monotonic grid paths using combinations, recognizing that a path is determined by which steps are chosen to be in a given direction.
questions.question: On a city grid, you can only move right or up, one block at a time. How many distinct shortest routes are there from one corner to a point that is 3 blocks right and 7 blocks up?
questions.explanation: Any shortest route consists of 3 "right" moves and 7 "up" moves in some order, so the number of routes equals the number of ways to place the right moves among all 10 moves: C(10,3) = 120.
questions.hint: A shortest path is just a sequence of right/up moves — choose which positions in that sequence are the right moves.

questions.learningObjective: Count derangements — permutations in which no element appears in its original position.
questions.question: 6 guests check their coats, and the coats are returned at random. In how many ways can the coats be returned so that no guest receives their own coat back?
questions.explanation: This asks for the number of derangements of 6 objects, denoted D(6). Using the known small derangement values D(1)=0, D(2)=1, D(3)=2, D(4)=9, D(5)=44, D(6)=265, D(7)=1854, we get D(6) = 265.
questions.hint: A permutation with no element in its original spot is called a derangement — recall or build up the small derangement numbers D(n).

questions.learningObjective: Count the number of distinct ways to arrange n distinct objects around a circle where rotations are considered identical.
questions.question: In how many distinct ways can 5 people be seated around a circular table, if seatings that are rotations of each other are considered the same?
questions.explanation: Fixing one person's seat to remove rotational duplicates, the remaining 4 people can be arranged in (5-1)! = 24 ways.
questions.hint: For circular arrangements, fix one object's position to account for rotational symmetry, then arrange the rest: (n−1)!.

questions.learningObjective: Use complementary counting to count arrangements where two specific objects must never be adjacent.
questions.question: 11 people, including Diego and Elena, are arranged in a row. In how many ways can they be arranged so that Diego and Elena are never next to each other?
questions.explanation: Total arrangements: 11! = 39916800. Arrangements with Diego and Elena adjacent (treated as a glued block): (11-1)! × 2 = 7257600. Subtracting: 39916800 − 7257600 = 32659200 arrangements keep them apart.
questions.hint: Find the total arrangements, then subtract the ones where the restricted pair is adjacent (complementary counting).

questions.concept: Permutations of r objects chosen from n
questions.learningObjective: Count ordered selections of r objects from a set of n distinct objects using P(n,r).
questions.question: 6 chess players compete in a race. In how many different ways can 1st and 2nd place be awarded, assuming no ties?
questions.explanation: Since the order of the 2 places matters, the count is P(6,2) = 6!/(6-2)! = 30.
questions.hint: When order matters (1st place differs from 2nd place), use the permutation formula P(n,r) = n!/(n−r)!.

questions.explanation: Since the two groups don't overlap and only one option is chosen, the addition principle gives 4 + 10 = 14 total choices.
questions.hint: When choices come from separate, non-overlapping groups and only one is picked, add the group sizes.

questions.explanation: Choose from each group independently and multiply: C(10,2) × C(8,3) = 45 × 56 = 2520.
questions.hint: Choose from each group separately using combinations, then multiply the two results together.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the coefficient of a specific term in a binomial expansion using binomial coefficients.
questions.question: In the binomial expansion of (1 + x)^7, what is the coefficient of the x^3 term?
questions.explanation: By the binomial theorem, (1+x)^7 = Σ C(7,k)·x^k, so the coefficient of x^3 is C(7,3) = 35.
questions.hint: In the expansion of (1+x)^n, the coefficient of x^k is exactly the binomial coefficient C(n,k).

questions.question: In a group of 32 students, 19 students do French and 16 students do Spanish. If 4 students do both, how many students do at least one of the two activities?

questions.learningObjective: Count the number of binary strings of a fixed length using the multiplication principle.
questions.question: How many distinct binary strings (sequences of 0s and 1s) of length 8 exist, representing a routing sequence?
questions.explanation: Each of the 8 positions independently can be 0 or 1, so by the multiplication principle there are 2^8 = 256 strings.
questions.hint: Each position has 2 independent choices (0 or 1); multiply the choices across all positions.

questions.explanation: Using stars and bars for identical items distributed with no minimum, the count is C(n+k−1, k−1) = C(10,2) = 45.
